ch01.note: The War of Resistance against Japan (1937–45), the Chinese name for the war set off by the Marco Polo Bridge Incident; from the Nationalist standpoint the central struggle of the age. Chen dates the events of his book by it.

Chen's central term is tewu gongzuo (特务工作), the covert operations of the Nationalist secret service: intelligence, sabotage, turning enemy agents, and targeted killing. The word tewu (secret agent) carries an unsavoury ring in Chinese, and his defence of the work is the theme of the third introduction.
The Chinese is huokou (活口), literally 'a living mouth': the one witness left alive to tell what happened, a phrase with an underworld chill.
Those who died for the state were honoured by having their tablets enshrined in a Martyrs' Shrine (忠烈祠) and by posthumous commendation.
The book's title, Yingxiong wuming (英雄无名), reads literally 'heroes, nameless': the men of the secret service who died unknown, their names in no history.

Chen projected the memoir in five books. Four were completed and are collected here; the fifth, on his own arrest and imprisonment in Shanghai, was never finished. This is the 'five-part plan' referred to later.

ch02.note: Dai Li (戴笠, 1897–1946), courtesy name Yunong (雨农), founder and lifelong head of the Nationalist secret service. A Whampoa man, he built the service from the early 1930s until his death in a 1946 air crash; feared and powerful, he is the presiding figure of Chen's story.

Chen gives dates by the Republican calendar, which counts from the founding of the Republic in 1912, so that Republican year n is 1911 + n (thus year 21 is 1932). Such dates are converted to the Western year throughout this translation.
Beiping ('Northern Peace') was the name of Beijing from 1928, when the Nationalists made Nanjing their capital, until 1949; it is called Beiping throughout the book.
The Kang-Ri Shajian Tuan (抗日杀奸团), a group of patriotic young people in occupied North China who assassinated collaborators.
An irregular anti-Japanese force in the Luan River and Shanhaiguan area of eastern Hebei (滦榆游击队).
A Station (站, zhan) was the service's local field office; Chen headed those at Beiping and Tianjin. A larger regional command was a District (区), such as the Shanghai District he later ran.
Zhang Jingyao (张敬尧, 1881–1933), a Beiyang-era general and former military governor of Hunan; assassinated in the Beiping Legation Quarter in 1933 for conspiring with the Japanese.
The Beiyang (北洋) clique, the military strongmen who dominated China between Yuan Shikai's death in 1916 and the Nationalist reunification of 1928.
The walled diplomatic quarter of Beiping, east of Tiananmen, where the foreign legations held extraterritorial rights and Chinese police could not enter.
Sun Chuanfang (孙传芳, 1885–1935), a major Beiyang warlord styled commander-in-chief of five provinces; broken by the Northern Expedition and later assassinated.
Shi Jianqiao (施剑翘) shot Sun Chuanfang dead in a Tianjin Buddhist hall in 1935 to avenge her father, whom Sun had executed; the celebrated case ended in a public pardon.

Ji Hongchang (吉鸿昌, 1895–1934), a former Northwest Army general who joined the 1933 Chahar anti-Japanese army; executed by the Nationalists in 1934. In the People's Republic he is honoured as a Communist martyr, the reverse of the account Chen gives here.
Feng Yuxiang (冯玉祥, 1882–1948), the 'Christian General,' a powerful and frequently-shifting warlord and a founder of the 1933 Chahar anti-Japanese army.
A former province of the North China and Inner Mongolian borderland, north-west of Beiping; abolished in 1952.

Chen writes in the Nationalist idiom, ascribing Ji Hongchang's revolt to Communist direction. Historians treat the Chahar anti-Japanese army as a broad united-front venture; Ji did join the Communist Party in 1932, but the flat attribution here is the memoir's partisan reading, not settled fact.
Shi Yousan (石友三, 1891–1940), a general notorious for switching allegiances again and again; killed by his own side in 1940.
Yin Rugeng (殷汝耕, 1885–1947), head of the Japanese-sponsored 'East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Government' (1935–38); tried and executed as a traitor after the war.
Wang Kemin (王克敏, 1879–1945), head of the Japanese puppet 'Provisional Government of the Republic of China' at Beiping; nicknamed 'Blind Wang' for his failing sight.
Bushido (武士道), 'the way of the warrior,' the Japanese samurai code of honour and willingness to die.

ch02.anchor: anyone may put them to death
ch02.note: A classical maxim in the Confucian tradition: rebellious ministers and unfilial sons are fair game for any hand. Chen invokes it to justify the killings as righteous.

ch03.note: A provisional English rendering of Chen's title for Book Two, Henei ru ming (河内辱命), roughly 'orders dishonoured at Hanoi.' He set that title aside; the book was published as The Full Story of the Wang Case at Hanoi (河内汪案始末), and he discusses his choice of titles in its Author's Preface.

Wang Jingwei (汪精卫, 1883–1944), a founding Nationalist leader and rival of Chiang Kai-shek who broke with Chongqing in December 1938 to seek peace with Japan and, from 1940, headed a Japanese-sponsored government at Nanjing. The 1939 attempt on his life at Hanoi is the subject of Book Two.
Then the capital of Tonkin in French Indochina, where Wang Jingwei took refuge after leaving Chongqing; foreign soil beyond Chinese jurisdiction.
Wang's so-called yan telegram (艳电, the yandian) of December 1938, which publicly urged a negotiated peace with Japan: his open break with the resistance.
A shuanghuang (双簧), a comic turn in which one performer mouths the words another speaks from behind: here the suspicion that Wang's 'defection' was staged in secret collusion with Chongqing.
Chongqing (重庆), in Sichuan, was the wartime capital of Nationalist China from 1938; the seat of the government committed to resistance.
Chen Bijun (陈璧君, 1891–1959), Wang Jingwei's wife and a forceful political figure in her own right; imprisoned after the war.

ch03.anchor: opening of the government at Nanjing
ch03.note: Wang Jingwei's Reorganized National Government, inaugurated at Nanjing in March 1940 under Japanese sponsorship, in rivalry with Chongqing.
The Hanoi action team. Chen names several of them here (Yu Jiansheng, Wang Luqiao, Tang Yingjie), whose parts fill the narrative of Book Two.

ch04.note: A District (区, qu) was a regional command of the service, larger than a Station; Chen was chief of the Shanghai District from 1939.

Throughout, 'the Juntong' renders 军统 / 军统局, short for the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission (军事委员会调查统计局), the Nationalists' military secret service under Dai Li. The full name dates strictly from 1938; Chen uses it loosely for the whole lineage that began with the Lixingshe's Special Services Department in 1932 (see the Prefatory Note), so its use for the earlier years is a mild anachronism.
'Sanction' renders 制裁 (zhicai), the service's own euphemism for the targeted killing or execution of a traitor or enemy; the term is kept throughout.
Fu Xiao'an (傅筱庵, 1872–1940), a banker installed as puppet mayor of Shanghai; assassinated in his bed in 1940 by his own cook, an agent of the resistance.
Zhang Xiaolin (张啸林), one of the 'Three Tycoons' of the Shanghai Green Gang, alongside Du Yuesheng and Huang Jinrong; killed in 1940 for collaborating with the Japanese.
Li Shiqun (李士群, 1905–1943), a former Communist who ran the Wang regime's secret police at No. 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai; poisoned by the Japanese in 1943.
The Wang regime's dreaded secret-police apparatus (特工总部), known from its address as 'No. 76.'
The Kempeitai (宪兵队), the Japanese army's military police, which ran counter-intelligence and repression in occupied China.
The Tokko (特高), the 'special higher police,' the Japanese political-police branch.
The Ume Kikan (梅机关, 'Plum Blossom Agency'), the Japanese special-service organ that engineered Wang Jingwei's defection and his Nanjing regime.
A former Tokkō officer of the Japanese military police at Nanjing whom Chen met again in Taipei in 1980. The Japanese reading of his name is reconstructed from the Chinese characters (大冢清).
From the Mencius: the mark of the 'great man' is that riches and honour cannot corrupt him, poverty and low estate cannot swerve him, power and force cannot bend him.
The radical clique led by Mao Zedong's wife Jiang Qing, blamed for the worst of the Cultural Revolution; arrested in 1976, a month after Mao's death.

Liu Shaoqi (刘少奇, 1898–1969), head of state of the People's Republic, purged and hounded to death during the Cultural Revolution; Tao Zhu (陶铸) was another senior victim. Chen notes with irony that the Communists branded their own fallen leaders 'Kuomintang secret agents.'

The Kaohsiung (Formosa) Incident of December 1979, a pro-democracy demonstration in Taiwan broken up by the Nationalist authorities and followed by mass trials. Chen, a career security man, writes of the dissidents with hostility.

Mao Zedong (毛泽东), leader of the Chinese Communist Party. Chen refers to him elsewhere as Mao qiu (毛酋), 'the Mao chieftain' or 'bandit chief Mao'; the Nationalist idiom that casts the Communist leadership as bandits is preserved throughout.
Lin Biao (林彪) and Nie Rongzhen (聂荣臻), the Communist commanders whose armies encircled and took Beiping and Tianjin in the winter of 1948–49.

'Pacification' (绥靖) and, later, 'suppression of the rebellion' (戡乱) are the Nationalist terms for the 1946–49 civil war, casting the Communists as rebels to be put down. They are kept as Chen's own idiom.

Zheng Jiemin (郑介民) and Mao Renfeng (毛人凤) headed the postwar secret service after Dai Li's death. The Bureau of Confidential Investigation (保密局, the Baomiju) was the Juntong's renamed successor from 1946.
The treaties imposed on China from the 1840s that granted foreign powers concessions and extraterritorial rights on Chinese soil: the legal reason Chinese police could not act inside the Concessions.
The foreign-run Shanghai International Settlement and the adjacent French Concession, self-governing enclaves outside Chinese jurisdiction.

An allusion to Zhang Liang's failed ambush of the First Emperor of Qin at Bolang, whose iron missile struck the wrong carriage: hence, killing the wrong man. It also titles a later chapter of the book.
Zeng Zhongming (曾仲鸣, 1896–1939), Wang Jingwei's close aide, killed at Hanoi in the attack meant for Wang.
From a Tang anecdote of a would-be hermit who won office by a show of reclusion on Mount Zhongnan; the phrase means a back-door route to a career.

ch05.note: The Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931, in which the Japanese army seized Manchuria: the opening of Japan's aggression against China.
The Shanghai Incident of 28 January 1932, a month of fighting between Japanese and Chinese forces around Shanghai.
The Nationalist officer academy near Guangzhou (founded 1924), whose graduates formed the core of Chiang Kai-shek's army and of the secret service; a 'Whampoa man' was one of this favoured clique.

ch05.anchor: the Three Principles of the People
ch05.note: Sun Yat-sen's political doctrine of Nationalism, Democracy, and the People's Livelihood (三民主义), the founding ideology of the Kuomintang.
The 'Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People' (三民主义力行社), a secret organization of Whampoa officers formed in 1932 and popularly known as the 'Blue Shirts.'
The covert-operations department (特务处) of the Lixingshe, directed by Dai Li: the operational seed from which the Juntong grew.
The bureau (调查统计局) set up under the Military Affairs Commission in 1932; its Second Department, under Dai Li, was the government-side face of the same secret-service work and grew into the Juntong.
A second-tier body (革命军人同志会) under the Lixingshe, one tier of the layered organization through which the secret service operated.

ch06.note: 'The Commandant' (校长) is Chiang Kai-shek, who as head of the Whampoa Military Academy and its Nanjing successor was addressed by his officers and cadets as 校长 for the rest of his life. Chen uses it, together with 'the Leader' (领袖) and 'the Generalissimo' (委员长, chairman of the Military Affairs Commission), throughout as reverent names for Chiang; 蒋公 is the honorific 'Mr. Chiang.'

The 中山装 (Zhongshan zhuang), the high-collared four-pocket tunic named for Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan) and known in the West as the 'Mao suit' from its later Communist use; in this period it was the plain everyday dress of Nationalist officials and officers.

ch06.anchor: Central Military Academy Special Research Class
ch06.note: The 中央军校 (Central Military Academy) was the Nanjing successor, from 1928, to the Whampoa Military Academy; its graduates are the 'academy classmates' who fill this book. The 'Special Research Class' was a small, hand-picked study group under its political department.

ch06.anchor: several books the Commandant himself had prescribed
ch06.note: The prescribed works are Neo-Confucian and statecraft classics: the collected works of Lu Xiangshan (Lu Jiuyuan, 1139-1193) and of Wang Yangming (1472-1529), the two great idealist philosophers of the mind; the collected works of Zeng Guofan (posthumous title Wenzheng, 1811-1872), the Qing statesman and general who suppressed the Taiping rebellion; and the military maxims of Qi Jiguang (1528-1588), the Ming general famed for defeating the coastal pirates. The last title is a modern exposition of Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People.
So called because the building's plan had the shape of the character 工 (gong) - an I-shape of two long halls joined by a shorter passage between.
中正 (Zhongzheng) is Chiang Kai-shek's formal given name, with which he signed official documents; the familiar 'Chiang Kai-shek' is the Cantonese reading of another of his names, 介石 (Jieshi).

The Whampoa Academy and its successor numbered their graduating classes (期, qi): the first class graduated in 1924, and seniority ran strictly by class, so that a man of an earlier class was an 'elder brother' (老大哥) to those of later ones. Chen was of the fifth class, Dai Li nominally of the sixth.
The yuan (元) was the silver dollar, the standard currency of Republican China; forty to eighty yuan was a modest but livable monthly stipend for a junior officer at this time.

Hu Hanmin (1879-1936), a leading Kuomintang theorist and rival of Chiang Kai-shek; Chiang's detention of him in 1931 touched off a revolt of the southern Guangdong-Guangxi leaders, whose anti-Chiang movement the book here calls a 'New Kuomintang.'
From the proverb 上有天堂，下有苏杭, 'Above there is Heaven; below, there are Suzhou and Hangzhou' - the two lower-Yangtze cities long held the fairest and most prosperous places on earth.
洪公祠, a shrine hall to a 'Lord Hong,' which gave its name to the training ground behind it; in Juntong lore the 'Honggongci Training Class' became the legendary cradle of the service's field officers.
The Cheka (切卡, from the Russian ChK) was the Soviet political police founded in 1917, forerunner of the OGPU, NKVD, and KGB, and a byword for the modern secret service.

Four brotherhoods of the Chinese underworld and secret-society world: the Sandianhui ('Three Dots Society,' a Triad branch) and the Gelaohui ('Elder Brothers Society') of the Yangtze provinces, and the Green Gang (青帮) and Red or Hong Gang (洪帮) - the last the great sworn-brotherhood networks of Republican Shanghai.

ch06.anchor: the eyes and ears of the Leader
ch06.note: 领袖耳目、兄弟手足 - a couplet Dai Li later composed as the motto of his service: its members were to be the eyes and ears of the Leader (Chiang) and hands and feet to one another.

The 中统 (Central Statistics Bureau of the Kuomintang's Organization Department) was the party's civilian secret service, grown from this Investigation Section and run by the Chen brothers' 'CC Clique'; it was the lifelong rival of Dai Li's military 'Juntong.'
阁子, Beiping dialect for the neighborhood police box or substation; literally a 'little pavilion.'
The Chinese Youth Party (中国青年党), founded 1923, a small nationalist and anti-Communist third party opposed alike to the Kuomintang and the Communists.
六国饭店, the 'Six Nations Hotel,' known in French as the Grand Hôtel des Wagons-Lits, a leading foreign hotel in the Legation Quarter of Beiping; it was there that Zhang Jingyao was shot.

On 4 June 1928 the Japanese Kwantung Army blew up the train of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin (the 'Old Marshal') at Huanggutun near Mukden, killing him; the deed opened the way to Japan's later seizure of the Northeast.
四公子, 'the Four Young Masters' - a loose epithet, varying in the telling, for the famous playboy sons of prominent Republican political and military families.

四维学会; the 四维 are the 'Four Cardinal Bonds' named by the ancient statesman Guan Zhong - 礼义廉耻, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and a sense of shame - which the Nationalists made a watchword of their New Life Movement.

In December 1936 Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng seized Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an and held him until he agreed to a united front with the Communists against Japan; Zhang was thereafter placed under a house arrest that lasted more than fifty years.

Itagaki Seishirō (1885-1948; the standard reading of 板垣, here written 坂垣), a general of the Japanese Kwantung Army and an architect of the 1931 seizure of Manchuria; later war minister, he was hanged as a war criminal in 1948.

The Baoding Military Academy (保定军官学校, 1912-1923), the principal training school for Chinese army officers before Whampoa; many senior commanders of the warlord and Nationalist armies were its graduates.

ch07.note: Rehe (热河), or Jehol, a former province of the mountainous borderland north-east of Beiping. In February–March 1933 the Japanese Kwantung Army overran it in a swift campaign (the “Operation Nekka”), annexing it to the puppet state of Manchukuo and carrying the fighting down to the passes of the Great Wall; the province was abolished in 1955.

Cai E (蔡锷, 1882–1916), the Yunnan general who in 1915 slipped out of Yuan Shikai’s Beijing—by popular legend with the help of the sing-song girl Xiao Fengxian (小凤仙), whose favours gave him his cover—to raise the National Protection War against Yuan’s attempt to make himself emperor. Their romance became a stock subject of opera, stage, and screen, which is the “Xiao Fengxian” Chen means.

The 八大胡同, a cluster of lanes just south of Qianmen that formed Beiping’s licensed pleasure quarter. The first-class houses advertised themselves as “pure-singing houses” (清吟小班), where in principle the women sold their song and their company rather than their bodies; 平康里 (Pingkangli) is a classical literary name for such a district.

打茶围, the custom of a paid introductory visit to a courtesan: the guest sits with her over tea, melon seeds, cigarettes, and talk, appraising her while she appraises his purse. It carried a set fee and, at a proper “home” room, formally opened the acquaintance; it implied nothing further of itself.
Zhang Zongchang (张宗昌, 1881–1932), warlord of Shandong, nicknamed the “Dog-Meat General,” a byword for brute cruelty, uncounted concubines, and buffoonery; driven out in 1928 and assassinated in 1932.

Manchukuo (满洲国), the puppet state Japan set up in the Northeast in 1932 under the last Qing emperor, Puyi. The Japanese aim Chen describes was to engineer a comparable client regime across North China—the project the Zhang Jingyao affair was part of.

ch07.anchor: The Secret Records of President Chiang
ch07.note: 蒋总统秘录, a documentary biography of Chiang Kai-shek drawn largely from Nationalist archives, serialized in Japan’s Sankei Shimbun in the mid-1970s and issued in Chinese translation by the Central Daily News (中央日报) in Taipei. Chen quotes the Chinese edition.

Duan Qirui (段祺瑞, 1865–1936), the Beiyang premier and head of the Anhui clique who dominated the Beijing government in the late 1910s; by 1933 long out of power and living in retirement, which is why the Japanese hoped to draw him out.

Song Zheyuan (宋哲元, 1885–1940), commander of the Twenty-Ninth Army in North China; his troops fought the Japanese at the Great Wall passes in 1933 and again at the Marco Polo Bridge in July 1937. Zhang Jingyao’s claim of “deep ties” to him, on which Itagaki paid out, appears to have been a boast.

ch07.anchor: A Tale of Heroic Sons and Daughters
ch07.note: 儿女英雄传, a mid-nineteenth-century novel by Wen Kang. Its heroine, Shisanmei (十三妹, “Thirteenth Sister”) He Yufeng, sets out to avenge her murdered father but is dissuaded before she can strike—hence Chen’s point that Shi Jianqiao, who did carry her revenge through, went a step further.

The Xinchou Treaty (辛丑条约) of 1901, imposed on the Qing by the eight allied powers after the Boxer Uprising. It fixed a vast indemnity and formalized the Legation Quarter as a walled, foreign-garrisoned enclave into which Chinese authority could not reach—the “humiliating brand” Chen names.

ch08.note: The Tanggu Truce (塘沽协定), signed 31 May 1933, ended the fighting that followed the Japanese seizure of Rehe and the Kwantung Army’s push to the Great Wall. It fixed a demilitarized zone across eastern Hebei from which Chinese forces were barred, leaving the approaches to Beiping and Tianjin under effective Japanese control. The Nationalist government presented it as a necessary breathing-space; its critics called it a surrender of sovereignty—the very charge Chen describes disaffected figures such as Feng Yuxiang seizing upon.

ch08.anchor: a pair of old men of the Green Gang
ch08.note: The Green Gang (青帮) was a sworn brotherhood and secret society, rooted among the boatmen of the Grand Canal and grown by the Republican era into a powerful criminal and political fraternity, strongest in the Yangtze cities. Members were ranked by fixed “generation” characters (here the “Tong” rank), and a senior man initiated new disciples in a formal ceremony called “opening the incense hall” (开香堂)—which is why a gathering of men with no women present was mistaken for a conspiratorial meeting.

The Peking Union Medical College (北平协和医学院), founded in 1906 and re-endowed from 1915 by the Rockefeller Foundation, was the most prestigious modern medical school in China; its degree marked an elite Western-trained physician.

The Mackenzie Memorial Hospital (马大夫纪念医院) in the British concession at Tianjin, named for the Scottish medical missionary John Kenneth Mackenzie; his surname, transliterated, gave the colloquial Chinese name “Dr. Ma” (马大夫).

ch08.anchor: The Lishunde Hotel is the first name in Tianjin
ch08.note: The Lishunde (利顺德大饭店), known in English as the Astor House Hotel, opened in the British concession in 1863 and was the oldest and grandest Western-style hotel in Tianjin, a byword for luxury and expense.

ch08.anchor: though I did not kill Boren
ch08.note: An allusion to the Book of Jin. The statesman Wang Dao, believing his friend Zhou Yi (styled Boren) had failed to defend him, let Zhou go to his execution unopposed; only afterward did he find the memorials in which Zhou had secretly pleaded for his life, and cried, “Though I did not kill Boren, Boren died because of me.” The phrase names a death one did not intend but must in conscience answer for.

The “Mauser” (驳壳枪) is the German C96 semi-automatic pistol, distinguished by its boxy fixed magazine and a detachable wooden holster that clips on as a shoulder-stock—hence the northern nicknames “box” (盒子) and “wood-shell” (木壳). Cheap, hard-hitting, and imported or copied in vast numbers, it was the signature sidearm of warlord China, of its bandits, and of its secret agents.

The “Blue Shirt Society” (蓝衣社) was the name by which outsiders—the press, the Japanese, and above all the Communists—knew the secret Nationalist fraternity that Chen calls the Lixingshe and the Renaissance Society. The label (from a supposed uniform) fastened on the organization a lurid reputation as Chiang Kai-shek’s fascist-style terror apparatus. Chen, writing from within, treats “Blue Shirts” as an enemy’s coinage; that Ji Hongchang should imagine himself dueling with it is, to him, a Communist fantasy.
The pun is on “red” (红): both the building’s red brick and the “red” Communist cause it secretly served.

ch08.anchor: I grieve I did not die resisting Japan
ch08.note: This five-word quatrain, said to have been written by Ji Hongchang on the execution ground, is honored in the People’s Republic as his martyr’s testament and is inscribed at his memorials. Chen, as an interested witness on the opposing side, doubts its authenticity and takes it for a posthumous Communist embellishment.

ch08.anchor: a great riot of "Red Guards" broke out at Zhengzhou
ch08.note: During the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) the “Red Guards” (红卫兵) were militant student factions first mobilized by Mao Zedong; by 1967–68 rival factions, some armed and backed by army units, fought pitched battles across China. Chen’s contemptuous “Mao hag” renders 毛婆, a jeer at Jiang Qing, Mao’s wife and a leader of the radical faction; Lin Biao was then Mao’s defense minister and designated successor.

The Dagongbao (大公报, “L’Impartial”), founded at Tianjin in 1902, was the most respected independent Chinese newspaper of the Republican era. The Shenbao (申报) cited just below was Shanghai’s leading daily.
